meta.report_title: Grupo Atlas Servicios Financieros — comprehensive fictional assessment
meta.report_subtitle: Channels, payments, identity, data and continuity / 60 findings and 7 notebooks

root_groups.name: Resource authorization and separation of duties
root_groups.cause: Policy applies to a channel or role but omits the resolved resource, organization or identity that approved its content.
root_groups.action: Centralize authorization by subject, operation, object and context; retain isolation and independent-identity checks.
root_groups.allowed: An identity from organization A reads or modifies its own case file using the current revision.
root_groups.rejected: The same identity attempts to act on a case file belonging to B or approve a decision it initiated; no state change is permitted.
root_groups.recovery: Repeat the decision after changing the resource or policy; an earlier approval must not authorize new content.

root_groups.name: Authentication and session lifecycle
root_groups.cause: Credentials, challenges, devices and sessions do not share a revocation policy and an operation identity.
root_groups.action: Bind each challenge to an intent, subject and validity period; verify the invalidation of all derived access.
root_groups.allowed: A valid session performs the exact operation for which the challenge was granted.
root_groups.rejected: An expired, consumed or operation-mismatched challenge must be rejected with a uniform response.
root_groups.recovery: Revoke the session and repeat reads and actions through all derived access paths before accepting closure.

root_groups.name: Consistency of monetary amounts and state transitions
root_groups.cause: A message identity, exchange-rate revision or isolated approval replaces the business obligation and its invariants.
root_groups.action: Model states, currencies and revisions explicitly; provide idempotency and compensation without concealing partial results.
root_groups.allowed: An authorized obligation produces a ledger entry with a consistent currency, amount and business revision.
root_groups.rejected: A duplicate message or incompatible transition must preserve the earlier result without a second effect.
root_groups.recovery: Interrupt the model between recording and confirmation; recover the obligation and demonstrate one explainable result.

root_groups.name: Documents, consent and purpose
root_groups.cause: Derived content remains accessible or is reused after consent, purpose or classification changes.
root_groups.action: Link revisions, purposes, recipients and revocations at every document consumer.
root_groups.allowed: An authorized recipient accesses only the attributes and revisions permitted for its purpose.
root_groups.rejected: Withdrawal of permission must block links, downloads, caches and derivatives of the same case file.
root_groups.recovery: Apply a revocation or classification change and check that all consumers converge on the new policy.

root_groups.name: Supply chain and approved changes
root_groups.cause: Review is associated with a name or pipeline run without establishing the identity of the deployed bytes, dependencies and configuration.
root_groups.action: Sign and verify artifact manifests, restrict promotion and retain a rollback path that respects current restrictions.
root_groups.allowed: The approved artifact matches its manifest and is promoted by an identity with a narrowly scoped function.
root_groups.rejected: Different content under the same name or an unapproved configuration must block the entire promotion.
root_groups.recovery: Roll back the model without reactivating secrets, permissions or dependencies retired after the earlier version.

root_groups.name: Effective privilege and administrative identity
root_groups.cause: Inherited permissions, service credentials and auxiliary channels extend the effective authority of monitoring or support roles.
root_groups.action: Evaluate effective permissions, separate control planes and remove unnecessary transitive authority while checking its operational impact.
root_groups.allowed: A read-only identity obtains only the information and operations described by its role.
root_groups.rejected: The same identity cannot modify groups, elevate privileges or retrieve an administrative credential.
root_groups.recovery: Refresh groups and tokens after withdrawing a delegation; check that the new policy also reaches existing sessions.

root_groups.name: Continuity with policy and integrity checks
root_groups.cause: A service is considered recovered when its bytes become available, without reconciling revocations, sequences or security dependencies.
root_groups.action: Recover content, state and restrictions as one unit; make reopening conditional on documented checks.
root_groups.allowed: An intact, authorized backup restores a known revision in an isolated environment.
root_groups.rejected: A backup with an incomplete manifest, stale state or missing controls must prevent reopening.
root_groups.recovery: Reconcile changes made after the backup and demonstrate that resuming service does not restore withdrawn access.

root_groups.name: Analytical data and automated decisions
root_groups.cause: Consumers reinterpret source units, times, identities or limitations and present results without preserving that uncertainty.
root_groups.action: Version data and model contracts; show provenance and limitations before automating a decision.
root_groups.allowed: A batch with a valid schema, units, date and provenance produces output traceable to its revision.
root_groups.rejected: A missing column, incompatible unit or unknown revision must produce an explicitly incomplete result.
root_groups.recovery: Reprocess a corrected batch without duplicating records or removing the explanation of earlier decisions.

root_groups.name: Audit records and verifiable evidence
root_groups.cause: Follow-up loses correlation, revision or time provenance and confuses a closure communication with evidence of an outcome.
root_groups.action: Retain stable identifiers, time provenance and evidence bound to specific criteria.
root_groups.allowed: An event explains who decided, which revision was involved and what happened, without including unnecessary data.
root_groups.rejected: Evidence without a revision or an undated note must not replace the latest verifiable result.
root_groups.recovery: Reconstruct a sequence across services and compare revision, correlation and limitations before declaring closure.

root_groups.name: Third parties, retention and trust boundaries
root_groups.cause: Integration or retirement processes retain alternative paths that do not respect the current supplier or data contract.
root_groups.action: Inventory consumers and derivatives; apply consistent limits and verify complete withdrawal of logical access.
root_groups.allowed: An active third party uses only the functions and data defined by its current mandate.
root_groups.rejected: A retired supplier or an expired derivative cannot continue reading or modifying resources.
root_groups.recovery: Simulate contract termination and recovery; verify revocation across queues, backups, indexes and pending tasks.

findings.title: Transfer batch accepts an order from another organization
findings.condition: The corporate channel checks that the operator may prepare batches but adds orders by global identifier. In the invented dataset, an order from contract B enters batch A without rechecking ownership or currency. The detail screen does apply the organization filter.
findings.consequence: Combining the batch could disclose or modify another organization’s order and mix payment decisions from two contracts. The scenario transfers no money.
findings.correction: Resolve each order within the server-side contract and authorize it before reserving funds; reject the entire batch if any resource fails a precondition.
findings.scenario: Two fictional companies own three orders each. Operator A prepares a valid two-order batch and a second, mixed batch containing a reference from B; the affected records and symbolic reservation are compared.

findings.title: Approval remains valid after the beneficiary is replaced
findings.condition: The second approval is bound to the request identifier even if the beneficiary changes later. The service retains the approved flag because the amount is unchanged. The earlier review contains neither the new destination nor its revision.
findings.consequence: Authorization of different content could be presented as current approval of a transfer. No real account numbers are used.
findings.correction: Bind approval to an immutable revision of the beneficiary, amount and currency; invalidate it after any relevant change and require renewed approval by an authorized identity.
findings.scenario: Two fictional recipients have the same amount. Approval covers DESTINO-A; changing the request to DESTINO-B must return it to a pending state.

findings.title: Balance export omits the account delegation mandate
findings.condition: Individual queries resolve the current mandate for each account. Export groups all company accounts based only on organization membership. An account for which the operator has no assigned authority appears in the example CSV.
findings.consequence: The synthetic batch reveals an account relationship and balance that the same subject cannot query individually. This scope is not extrapolated to other exports.
findings.correction: Share the authorization predicate across queries, aggregation and export; resolve authority by account and decision time.
findings.scenario: A company has operating, reserve and collateral accounts. The operator has authority over the first two; the control compares batch rows with individual account queries.

findings.title: Supervisor approves their own exception through another channel
findings.condition: The main interface prevents approval of one’s own request, but an auxiliary queue compares session identifiers rather than the stable subject. The same fictional person opens another session, which is represented as independent approval.
findings.consequence: Apparent separation of duties does not ensure a second independent decision. The model neither demonstrates real fraud nor attributes intent to people.
findings.correction: Enforce incompatibility by stable identity and role; evaluate delegated accounts, substitute roles and different sessions against the same policy.
findings.scenario: Requester S uses two synthetic sessions. Identity T may review the case file, whereas S must be rejected through both channels even after switching sessions.

findings.title: Shared loan exposes documents of a former co-borrower
findings.condition: A case file retains a document reference for a former co-borrower. A change in ownership updates the participants screen, but the attachments tab resolves the file through permission inherited from the original case file.
findings.consequence: An earlier relationship could retain document access outside the current contract. The example identities, documents and relationships are invented.
findings.correction: Evaluate rights by document, participant and validity period; remove derived references and permissions when ownership changes.
findings.scenario: The case file changes from A+B to A+C. The matrix keeps A’s own document, removes B’s document and gives C access only to documents authorized by the new relationship.

findings.title: Read-only role changes limits through a compound action
findings.condition: Policy permits reading the payment configuration, and the same endpoint accepts an update action in its body. The control is expressed by route and method rather than by the compound operation selected after routing.
findings.consequence: The model permits changes to an operational threshold from a role intended only for monitoring. No customer limits were changed.
findings.correction: Authorize the resolved action and separate read and change operations; validate permissions after interpreting the business command.
findings.scenario: An inert read request preserves the fictional limit. A second input with an update action must be rejected even when it uses the same route and identity.

findings.title: Session revocation does not reach derived mobile credentials
findings.condition: Ending the session invalidates the access token, but a mobile refresh credential remains active in another record. The model permits a new session after administrative removal of the device.
findings.consequence: Revocation might leave derived capabilities active and extend access for an excluded device. No usable tokens were generated.
findings.correction: Bind sessions and refresh credentials to a revocable family; check current status on refresh and eliminate races between refresh and withdrawal.
findings.scenario: Family A, a short-lived token and a long-lived refresh credential are created with values marked as synthetic. After family revocation, both paths must reject access and create no new session.

findings.title: Confirmation challenge can be reused for a second operation
findings.condition: The confirmation challenge is marked valid for a time window without being bound to the specific intent. Two invented transfers in different currencies present the same challenge, and the second inherits the first decision.
findings.consequence: Proof of possession could authorize an operation different from the one shown to the user. The document contains no codes from a real provider.
findings.correction: Bind the challenge to a hash of the relevant content, subject and operation; consume it atomically and reject any reuse.
findings.scenario: Intent A and intent B share a subject but differ in currency and recipient. Only A matches the confirmed representation; B must require an independent challenge.

findings.title: Password change preserves delegated support sessions
findings.condition: Recovery revokes interactive sessions but excludes delegated sessions created by support. The modeled record does not distinguish a current support mandate from a copy of permission issued before the password change.
findings.consequence: Delegated access could survive a recovery intended to remove suspicious access. No other person’s sessions were accessed.
findings.correction: Define explicit revocation of delegations and derived credentials during recovery; retain only justified, visible exceptions.
findings.scenario: The scenario compares an owner session, a current temporary delegation and a delegation from the previous period. Changing control of the account requires reevaluating all three.

findings.title: Recovery limit is calculated only by browser
findings.condition: The local counter belongs to a browser identifier rather than an account, challenge and intent. Several fabricated inputs change that identifier and stay below the local maximum while sharing the same example account.
findings.consequence: The policy could permit more attempts than intended and disrupt legitimate use. No email or SMS was sent.
findings.correction: Combine limits by account, operation and context with uniform responses; provide a legitimate recovery path without trivial budget resets.
findings.scenario: Five attempts from three browser identifiers are modeled against one challenge. The operation counter must increase consistently without depending on the client label.

findings.title: Mobile cache retains receipts after a profile change
findings.condition: The cache is indexed by device and date even though one device can switch between profiles. Signing out clears the main screen, but the offline view retains a receipt from the previous profile.
findings.consequence: Switching users could reveal another user’s locally stored document. All case images and references were created for this exercise.
findings.correction: Separate storage by identity and encrypt it with revocable keys; remove content on sign-out or profile change and check process restart and offline use.
findings.scenario: Profiles A and B share fictional device T. A saves a receipt and signs out, then B signs in offline; A’s document must remain inaccessible.

findings.title: Recovery message distinguishes a nonexistent account
findings.condition: Two prepared responses show different text for a registered alias and a nonexistent one. The channel also presents a different internal code. No timing is measured and no users are enumerated.
findings.consequence: The difference provides a limited existence signal; it does not by itself demonstrate access to the account or its attributes.
findings.correction: Make public output and help paths uniform, keep details in restricted records and also review the codes consumed by the mobile application.
findings.scenario: Exactly two synthetic aliases known to the author are compared. The contract requires the same public structure without claiming timing equivalence that was never measured.

findings.title: Payment retry creates a new obligation when the message changes
findings.condition: The engine prevents duplicate transport identifiers but accepts a different identifier for the same obligation. After confirmation is lost, the application resends the same business data in a new message, producing two symbolic ledger entries in the example.
findings.consequence: A single intent could be recorded twice and require manual compensation. Amounts are invented units without a banking connection.
findings.correction: Define idempotency by obligation and transition; reserve and confirm within an atomic boundary, returning the earlier result for equivalent retries.
findings.scenario: Obligation O-001 for 125 units produces message M1. Confirmation is lost, and M2 retains the obligation and amount; the expected ledger contains only one net effect.

findings.title: Clearing uses a different exchange rate from authorization
findings.condition: Authorization stores the original amount, whereas clearing recalculates the conversion using the latest rate. The revision change between those steps is neither recorded as an adjustment nor subject to a business decision.
findings.consequence: The model can produce differences that resemble rounding but actually reflect another rate. It does not represent real market prices.
findings.correction: Bind the operation to an exchange-rate revision and rounding rules; model adjustments as separate authorized transitions.
findings.scenario: A synthetic operation converts currency X into Y at rate V1. V2 appears before clearing; the control requires retaining V1 or explicitly recording a new authorization.

findings.title: Partial refund ignores simultaneous reservations
findings.condition: Two refund requests read the same available balance before reserving it. Each request fits within the original amount on its own, but together they exceed it. Validation occurs outside the update to the cumulative amount.
findings.consequence: The fictional race could refund more than the authorized amount and make reconciliation impossible without later adjustments.
findings.correction: Reserve and apply refunds through an atomic condition on the remaining balance; retain idempotency keys and trace reservation releases.
findings.scenario: The symbolic purchase is worth 100 units. Concurrent requests for 70 and 50 must yield one acceptance and one rejection, or follow an explicit, documented partial-refund policy.

findings.title: Late cancellation leaves a funds reservation unreleased
findings.condition: The request state changes to canceled, but release is sent as an event without durable confirmation. If the consumer does not process it, the reservation continues reducing the available balance even though no active order exists.
findings.consequence: The inconsistency could immobilize fictional funds and generate complaints. It demonstrates neither monetary loss nor a failure in a real system.
findings.correction: Maintain a reconcilable transition between cancellation and reservation; allow idempotent retries and alert on incompatible states.
findings.scenario: The model is interrupted after cancellation and before release. On resumption, reconciliation must detect the orphaned reservation and resolve it exactly once.

findings.title: Per-line rounding differs from the settlement total
findings.condition: Lines are rounded to the smallest currency unit, whereas the total uses extended precision before rounding. A small set of fractional amounts creates a difference that is neither assigned to an account nor explained to the consumer.
findings.consequence: The result makes differences difficult to reconcile and attribute, even when each calculation appears reasonable in isolation.
findings.correction: Document precision, rounding point and rounding rule; retain the original amount, result and explicit adjustment, with boundary checks.
findings.scenario: Three lines of 0.005 units are modeled, comparing their sum with the rounded total. The contract must unambiguously define which value is published and why.

findings.title: Late order is processed under the wrong calendar
findings.condition: The operational cutoff interprets a local date without a time zone, while the consumer converts it from UTC. Around the day boundary, a fabricated order enters different batches depending on which component evaluates it. The calendars belong to the scenario.
findings.consequence: An operation could be assigned to a different processing day, changing reconciliation expectations. No real regulatory obligation is interpreted.
findings.correction: Specify the time zone, calendar, cutoff instant and rule revision; store the decision result with its provenance.
findings.scenario: One order is placed on each side of a fictional cutoff. Producer and consumer must choose the same batch using the same rule, even when the instant is represented in another time zone.

findings.title: Withdrawn consent remains active in deferred jobs
findings.condition: The API checks consent when creating a job, but the consumer executes hours later without reevaluating validity. The scenario withdraws permission between those steps, and the job retains a copy of its initially authorized state.
findings.consequence: Extraction could occur after the purpose that authorized it has been withdrawn. No real financial data was queried.
findings.correction: Version consent and reevaluate applicable conditions at consumption; explicitly define which previously accepted jobs must be canceled.
findings.scenario: Job J1 is created under permission V3. Before consumption, V4 records revocation; output must show cancellation or a previously defined, visible exception.

findings.title: Reclassified document retains a long-lived download link
findings.condition: The file changes from shareable to restricted, but the previously issued link checks only its own expiry date. Current classification is not part of download authorization.
findings.consequence: The recipient could continue retrieving a revision that should no longer be distributed. The example link points to a reserved domain.
findings.correction: Evaluate current permission and classification before serving each revision; limit validity and support revocation of an individual link.
findings.scenario: A link is issued for V1, and the case file is reclassified before it expires. A later read must be rejected, retaining an audit reason without publishing the file.

findings.title: Open finance returns attributes outside the consent purpose
findings.condition: Field selection is defined by product rather than consent purpose. In the example, balance-query permission also includes internal labels and contacts that the customer did not authorize for that purpose.
findings.consequence: The synthetic response contains more attributes than necessary. It demonstrates neither an actual leak nor noncompliance with a specific standard.
findings.correction: Define minimal schemas by purpose and revision; check both required-field presence and unauthorized-field absence.
findings.scenario: Two purposes are compared: balance aggregation and transaction reconciliation. Each output has an explicit set of attributes; adding an unknown field must fail visibly.

findings.title: Thumbnails and search survive document withdrawal
findings.condition: The process withdraws the main file but not its thumbnail or search-index excerpt. Derivatives keep responding under an old policy because they do not share a lifecycle reference.
findings.consequence: The model prolongs the availability of part of a document after its logical withdrawal. It does not claim irrecoverable physical erasure.
findings.correction: Inventory derivatives and propagate access withdrawal and deletion; check each consumer and retain justified exceptions.
findings.scenario: Document D has an original, a thumbnail, indexed text and a temporary copy. The matrix requires an outcome for each derivative instead of treating deletion of the original as complete closure.

findings.title: Document approval does not change when an annex is replaced
findings.condition: The acceptance mark is associated with the case-file ID. Replacing an annex with another file of the same name leaves that mark intact, even when the bytes and hash differ.
findings.consequence: A reader might attribute acceptance to new content without a corresponding review. No real electronic signature is used.
findings.correction: Bind acceptance to the component manifest and hashes; invalidate it when any relevant annex is replaced and show the accepted revision.
findings.scenario: The case file includes approved annex A1. A2 has the same name and different content; acceptance must become pending while evidence of the earlier review is retained.

findings.title: Image metadata exposes a synthetic internal note
findings.condition: An exported image retains a descriptive field created during editing. It is not visible in the displayed image, but the publication contract requires removal of that marker. The test literal is invented and deliberately recognizable.
findings.consequence: Distributing the original could reveal a note that does not belong in the deliverable. No real location or personal information is included.
findings.correction: Separate the private original from the publishable derivative; check metadata and references in each export using known control markers.
findings.scenario: The image contains a private marker in Description and public visual content. The report must use the sanitized derivative while the editable project retains the original for traceability.

findings.title: Artifact promotion approves a name without verifying its bytes
findings.condition: Deployment authorization identifies a file by name and label. Two different inert packages share those fields. The process does not compare the approved hash with the bytes consumed by final promotion.
findings.consequence: An unreviewed change could be presented as the approved version. The exercise downloads or executes no software packages.
findings.correction: Verify the manifest, hash, signature and dependencies before promotion; prevent partial promotion after any discrepancy and record the result.
findings.scenario: Manifests A and B have the same version name and different hashes. Only content matching the approved manifest may proceed.

findings.title: Review pipeline retains publication permissions
findings.condition: A job intended to validate changes also has permission to publish artifacts. Its effective identity is shared with the delivery job and is not restricted according to event type or source trust.
findings.consequence: A review boundary could reach publication functions it does not need. No untrusted code was executed and no real credential was used.
findings.correction: Separate identities and permissions by phase; grant publication only to verified delivery and check effective permissions for every event type.
findings.scenario: The model compares review, build and publication. Review needs only read access and results; a write request from that phase must be rejected by policy.

findings.title: Configuration added after signing changes the service destination
findings.condition: The binary has an approved manifest, but configuration is inserted later and is not covered by the same review. The example integration destination changes without invalidating acceptance of the assembled system.
findings.consequence: Executable identity does not establish the identity of the deployed system or its destinations. None of those destinations is contacted.
findings.correction: Include relevant configuration and secret policy in the delivery manifest; verify the complete assembly before activation.
findings.scenario: Approved configuration C1 points to reserved destination A. C2 changes it to reserved destination B; both use the same binary, but only the approved assembly may be accepted.

findings.title: Rollback reinstalls a retired dependency
findings.condition: Rollback selects the last stable version without reconciling the retired-component catalog. A dependency previously excluded by an internal decision reappears in the earlier package even though the reason for exclusion remains valid.
findings.consequence: Operational rollback can reintroduce an expired exception and lose the risk context. No specific vulnerability in a real component is claimed.
findings.correction: Apply current restrictions to rollback packages as well; prepare compatible fallback versions and retain exceptions with expiry dates.
findings.scenario: Version V2 retires fictional component X. When returning to V1, the control must detect X and either block rollback or use a previously reviewed fallback package.

findings.title: Build record mixes provenance from two runs
findings.condition: The manifest uses the current run ID, but a cache supplies an artifact from another revision. Evidence combines a recent identifier with old bytes and omits the origin link for the reused component.
findings.consequence: Apparent traceability can attribute checks to content that never underwent them. No actual build is called into question.
findings.correction: Record provenance per component and verify input, cache and output revisions; distinguish rebuilding from verified reuse.
findings.scenario: Run B reuses an output from A. The manifest must retain both identities and demonstrate that the reused content matches the authorized inputs.

findings.title: Inventory distinguishes active components from example material
findings.condition: The synthetic catalog identifies active dependencies, test tools and demonstration files with separate owners. This positive observation exercises zero scoring and avoids treating every repository file as executed code.
findings.consequence: No security impact is assigned. The existence of a dependency or example does not itself establish exposure.
findings.correction: Retain purpose, location, owner and review date; remove items only after checking their consumers confirms that they are unnecessary.
findings.scenario: The catalog contains active component A, test tool T and example E. Each has a different consumer and a defensible retention decision.

findings.title: Directory inheritance grants control over a privileged group
findings.condition: An inventory account inherits modification permission over a unit containing administrative groups. Review considers the direct ACL but not transitive delegation or object ownership.
findings.consequence: The lower-trust role could modify an administrative boundary in the model. No directory was contacted and no credentials were captured.
findings.correction: Evaluate effective permissions and inheritance, separate objects by function and check allowed reads together with rejected modifications.
findings.scenario: The fictional tree contains Inventory, Operations and Administration. The read-only account queries device attributes but cannot change group members or owners.

findings.title: Service credential permits interactive use on the jump host
findings.condition: An identity intended for a scheduled task retains an interactive access method. The service review lists its application permissions but omits logon rights on the jump host.
findings.consequence: A service credential would have broader authority than the operation for which it was granted. There are no real passwords or sessions.
findings.correction: Restrict logon types, separate task and administrative credentials and verify effective permissions by host and channel.
findings.scenario: Identity S performs a declared task in the model. The same subject must be rejected when requesting an interactive session or an administrative function outside that task.

findings.title: Privileged session outlives its temporary authorization
findings.condition: Temporary permission is removed from the catalog at the scheduled time, but an existing session retains its capabilities until manually closed. The system does not communicate expiry to the consumer of the original decision.
findings.consequence: The effective administration window can exceed the approved period. No access to any platform was maintained.
findings.correction: Bind the session to its grant and reevaluate validity for sensitive actions; terminate or reduce capabilities when authorization expires.
findings.scenario: Grant G expires at a fixed instant in the scenario. An earlier action is permitted, while the same action after expiry must be rejected even if the session identifier is unchanged.

findings.title: Backup role can retrieve administrative secrets
findings.condition: The backup function needs to copy encrypted content, but the operator identity also holds the decryption key and an export path. The model does not separate custody of bytes from use of the secret.
findings.consequence: An operational function could reach secrets it does not need to know. All values in the case are unusable markers.
findings.correction: Separate copying, restoration and decryption through different identities; restrict export and record authorization for a specific revision.
findings.scenario: Operator O can copy container C, while only authorized process R can restore it to an allowed destination. O must remain unable to obtain the contents.

findings.title: Group change does not update the support session
findings.condition: The session loads a group list at startup and does not check its revision afterward. Removing a role correctly restricts new sessions, but existing sessions continue presenting stale authorization.
findings.consequence: Permission withdrawal may remain incomplete for the life of a session. The example does not estimate a real exposure duration.
findings.correction: Version authorization and define session invalidation or per-action reevaluation; check differences between new and existing sessions.
findings.scenario: Group Extended-Support is removed from subject A. Earlier session S1 and later session S2 must converge on the same effective permissions before withdrawal is declared complete.

findings.title: Inventory exposes internal names in authorization errors
findings.condition: A rejection response contains invented group names and internal paths. It is presented to a user without an operational role even though those details are unnecessary to correct the request.
findings.consequence: The message reduces uncertainty about the model’s structure without demonstrating an exploitable chain or additional access.
findings.correction: Return an incident identifier and retain technical detail in restricted records; review successful responses, denials and internal failures.
findings.scenario: The rejected request produces a stable public code and correlation identifier. ACL detail remains only in the scenario’s diagnostic record.

findings.title: Reopening restores permissions revoked after the backup
findings.condition: The backup contains permissions valid at its creation time. Recovery restores those permissions without applying a later revocation record, and the service is considered ready when files become available again.
findings.consequence: Reopening could reactivate access that the business had withdrawn. Byte availability does not demonstrate policy recovery.
findings.correction: Reconcile revocations and classification changes before reopening; include allowed and rejected access cases in recovery criteria.
findings.scenario: Backup C1 predates the removal of supplier P. After restoration, P must still have no access even if it appears in the content’s historical ACLs.

findings.title: Partial backup is accepted without checking every manifest object
findings.condition: The job reports success because the main index was restored. Some required objects are missing and others belong to an earlier revision, but the complete inventory is not compared with the manifest hashes.
findings.consequence: Apparent recovery could leave case files incomplete or combine incompatible revisions. The model lost no real data.
findings.correction: Verify completeness, size and hash for every required member; distinguish partial recovery from acceptance and block incompatible consumers.
findings.scenario: The manifest lists three objects. The trial backup omits one and changes another; the expected result details both discrepancies and keeps reopening blocked.

findings.title: Restored queue reprocesses payments already cleared
findings.condition: The queue comes from a backup older than the restored ledger. On resumption, it contains intents whose effects already exist in the ledger, and the consumer assumes a pending message represents new work.
findings.consequence: Recovery could duplicate business effects even when both components are individually intact.
findings.correction: Reconcile queue positions with durable obligations; reuse business idempotency and record messages discarded because an earlier result exists.
findings.scenario: The ledger records obligation O as completed, and the queue contains its original message. Reopening must recognize O, preserve its ledger entry and produce no second effect.

findings.title: Failover starts two writers without a shared authority
findings.condition: The alternate node activates when it stops observing the primary. The primary remains reachable by part of the model, and both accept changes without an authority token that orders writes.
findings.consequence: Two state histories could diverge and require reconciliation of incompatible decisions. No real service was interrupted.
findings.correction: Use versioned write authority with fencing; reject operations issued under old grants and demonstrate convergence before reopening.
findings.scenario: Writers A and B share the same symbolic dataset. The new grant to B invalidates A’s earlier grant even when A does not receive immediate notification.

findings.title: Backup catalog omits the restoration-test outcome
findings.condition: The catalog shows date, size and backup success, but not whether isolated restoration met the reopening criteria. The screen presents backup availability as verified recovery.
findings.consequence: An operational decision could rely on evidence that is more limited than its label suggests.
findings.correction: Separate creation, integrity, restoration and acceptance; show the outcome, scope, date and limitations of each stage.
findings.scenario: A valid backup without a restoration test remains unverified. Another with partial restoration shows pending components and is not presented as ready for reopening.

findings.title: Continuity manual retains an incomplete version reference
findings.condition: A procedure reference loses its version parameter when copied into a table. The text remains readable, but the destination no longer identifies the same revision approved in the scenario.
findings.consequence: An operator might consult instructions for another version, making the procedure harder to reproduce. The observation does not claim a defect in report-gen.
findings.correction: Separate the visible label from the structured destination; verify exact preservation of parameters, fragments and international characters.
findings.scenario: A long URL with encoded parameters and a Unicode fragment is retained. The table, finding reference and narrative link must preserve the same complete destination.

findings.title: Analytics merges customers with the same name using a non-unique key
findings.condition: The batch uses a visible label as a global identity. Two invented customers share a trading name, and the consumer aggregates their transactions without including a contract or source identifier. A provenance column exists but does not participate in the join.
findings.consequence: Aggregation could attribute transactions and decisions to the wrong case file. No real names or transactions were processed.
findings.correction: Define stable composite keys and reject ambiguous joins; retain original values and provenance for each row.
findings.scenario: Contracts A and B use the label Central Trading. The join must keep two distinct subjects and flag references without a contract instead of choosing one arbitrarily.

findings.title: Fraud model uses a version different from the approved one
findings.condition: The decision retains a model label, while the service loads the latest version under that name. Parameters change without the decision record identifying their bytes or the effective threshold.
findings.consequence: An alert explanation could refer to a model different from the one that produced it. The case neither measures accuracy nor makes judgments about real people.
findings.correction: Record an immutable version, parameters and threshold for each decision; promote models through review bound to their content.
findings.scenario: Decision D1 is calculated with model M1 and D2 with M2. Documentary reproduction must show both contracts and prevent a shared label from concealing their differences.

findings.title: Late data replaces the current state of a decision
findings.condition: The consumer orders updates by arrival rather than source revision. A delayed batch overwrites newer case-file attributes, although it retains an earlier time in a column that is not consulted.
findings.consequence: The presented state could describe a different moment from the one used for the decision, producing inconsistent reviews.
findings.correction: Distinguish event time, receipt time and sequence; retain history and explicitly define how delayed or duplicate batches are handled.
findings.scenario: The case file receives revision 5 and then revision 4. Revision 4 is retained as a late event but must not silently replace current state 5.

findings.title: Unit conversion changes an alert threshold
findings.condition: One producer expresses amounts in minor units and another in whole units. The schema accepts both as numbers, and the consumer applies the same threshold without checking currency, scale or contract revision.
findings.consequence: The model can trigger or suppress alerts because of an incorrect implicit conversion. No actual effectiveness is attributed to a fraud-monitoring system.
findings.correction: Type currency and scale, normalize explicitly and reject inputs without units; record both original and normalized values.
findings.scenario: An input of 10000 hundredths and another of 100 whole units represent the same amount. Their decisions should be equivalent only after a declared, verifiable conversion.

findings.title: Missing field is interpreted as zero in an executive indicator
findings.condition: An incomplete batch lacks a required counter. The dashboard replaces absence with zero and presents the period as complete. The scenario distinguishes observed zero from data not received, but presentation loses that difference.
findings.consequence: An executive reader might interpret missing information as an absence of events and prioritize incorrectly.
findings.correction: Model completeness for each indicator; propagate unknown values and explain denominators before calculating percentages or trends.
findings.scenario: Period A contains zero confirmed events, and B lacks a source. The report must show zero for A and incomplete information for B without combining the two categories.

findings.title: Quality metrics specify denominators and excluded samples
findings.condition: The quality record declares received, accepted, rejected and pending counts, together with the denominator rule. It is included as a management observation to exercise tables and states without asserting a vulnerability.
findings.consequence: No technical impact is assigned. An indicator with visible scope does not establish universal quality or the validity of other metrics.
findings.correction: Keep the definition alongside the value, retain exclusion reasons and version any denominator change.
findings.scenario: A batch of 120 records contains 100 accepted, 12 rejected and 8 pending records. Proportions must identify whether their base is all received records or only evaluated records.

findings.title: Correlation is lost across the reconciliation queue
findings.condition: The producer records a stable obligation, but the consumer replaces that correlation with a temporary execution ID. Events exist, yet they do not distinguish a retry from an independent intent without inference.
findings.consequence: Reconstructing the model could combine different decisions or count retries as new operations. Loss of records is not claimed.
findings.correction: Preserve business correlation and add segment identifiers; record transitions and outcomes without copying full sensitive bodies.
findings.scenario: Obligation O passes through receipt, queue and ledger entry with two retries. Each segment retains O and its own identifier so the sequence can be explained unambiguously.

findings.title: Support redaction does not reach nested fields
findings.condition: The rule removes a marker at the top level, but a nested copy remains in the error message. Support exports both fields, and the public derivative includes the literal created to test isolation.
findings.consequence: The record could publish unnecessary content within the scenario. The marker is neither a credential nor personal information.
findings.correction: Define allowed fields and sanitize before storage and export; check nested objects, errors and derived views.
findings.scenario: The same synthetic marker appears in a simple key and in an array of details. Publication must remove it from both places while preserving a nonsensitive correlation.

findings.title: Closure evidence belongs to an earlier revision
findings.condition: The image is linked to the finding ID but not to the behavior revision. After a configuration change, closure retains the earlier capture and presents it alongside the new state without a warning.
findings.consequence: Evidence can imply verification that does not apply to the reviewed content. An image alone does not demonstrate remediation.
findings.correction: Bind evidence, hash, revision, date and criterion; mark it historical when a relevant precondition changes.
findings.scenario: Evidence E1 belongs to revision 2, while the finding is already at revision 3. Closure requires a new check or an explicit limitation rather than reusing E1 as current proof.

findings.title: Clock offset reverses authorization and execution in the record
findings.condition: Two scenario components use wall clocks with a known offset. The view sorts by that time and places execution before authorization, although the causal sequence differs and is available in another field.
findings.consequence: Reading the record can make a decision harder to explain. A visually precise timestamp establishes neither synchronization nor causal order.
findings.correction: Store time source, drift and logical sequence; distinguish event, receipt and presentation times when reconstructing operations.
findings.scenario: Authorization has sequence 10 and execution sequence 11, but their clocks differ. The result preserves both timestamps and uses the declared sequence to explain the relationship.

findings.title: Communicated acceptance appears as verified remediation
findings.condition: The workflow converts the word resolved in a communication into closed status. It requires no retest date, criterion or outcome, and risk acceptance ends up sharing the label used for verified remediation.
findings.consequence: Follow-up could confuse business decisions with technical evidence and hide pending work.
findings.correction: Separate communication, acceptance, reported remediation and verification; require evidence and limitations for each closure transition.
findings.scenario: Three records represent a communicated change, accepted risk and a successful retest. They must retain distinct states instead of automatically collapsing into a single resolved category.

findings.title: Follow-up retains a partial result and an undated note
findings.condition: The example log keeps a dated partial retest and a later, undated note. Presentation order neither makes the note the latest result nor removes the retest limitation.
findings.consequence: No technical impact is assigned. The observation checks that follow-up can express uncertainty without presenting it as approval.
findings.correction: Retain original records and select status through explicit date and outcome rules; do not infer closure from a narrative note.
findings.scenario: Retest R1 verifies two of three conditions; N1 adds undated context. Status remains partial until a dated result covers the remaining condition.

findings.title: Retired supplier retains authorized messages in the queue
findings.condition: Receipt validates a current mandate and stores the message. The supplier is later removed, but a worker processes the copied authorization without checking current status or the pending-operation contract.
findings.consequence: The model could permit changes after third-party access has been withdrawn. The treatment of already accepted messages requires an explicit business decision.
findings.correction: Version mandates and define which operations may finish; reevaluate validity and idempotently cancel those that are no longer authorized.
findings.scenario: Supplier P issues J1 before withdrawal and J2 afterward. J2 is immediately rejected; J1 is resolved under a documented rule that does not depend on an implicit permission copy.

findings.title: Supplier account changes settlement destination without dual control
findings.condition: The supplier account can modify the destination and confirm the change from a second screen. Both channels resolve the same subject, and a previous review remains valid even after the data changes.
findings.consequence: Separate screens do not ensure independent review of high-impact data. No real bank accounts exist in the case.
findings.correction: Require another authorized identity and bind approval to the exact revision; invalidate confirmations whenever a relevant field changes.
findings.scenario: Identity P requests a change from DESTINO-A to DESTINO-B. P cannot confirm the same change, and review T must explicitly identify destination B.

findings.title: Third-party delivery includes a column removed from the contract
findings.condition: The export schema evolves but retains an old column no longer permitted by the new mandate. The consumer accepts additional columns and does not detect that the dataset exceeds the current purpose.
findings.consequence: The synthetic batch distributes an unnecessary attribute. The exercise uses no real data and interprets no legal obligation.
findings.correction: Define an allowed schema by contract and revision; validate the absence of retired columns and record purpose changes.
findings.scenario: Revision 1 allows columns A, B and C. Revision 2 allows only A and B; a batch containing C must be rejected or sanitized through an explicit decision before distribution.

findings.title: Retention deletes the index without withdrawing temporary objects
findings.condition: The process deletes the main catalog entry, but a temporary job retains copies under a different naming convention. Closure counts deleted rows without inspecting those objects or their permissions.
findings.consequence: Scenario content can remain available through a derivative omitted from the inventory.
findings.correction: Link temporary copies to their source and policy; check logical withdrawal across all stores and explain the limits of physical deletion.
findings.scenario: Object D has a primary copy, an export temporary copy and a search excerpt. The control records an outcome for each derivative and leaves any unchecked consumer pending.

findings.title: Test origin remains allowed in the third-party portal
findings.condition: Stable configuration inherits a laboratory origin, and error responses use a list different from successful responses. Every URL in the document is reserved and was not queried.
findings.consequence: Policy extends unnecessary trust within the model. Impact depends on the methods, credentials and content actually exposed.
findings.correction: Derive policy by environment and centralize enforcement; check allowed, rejected and null origins in successful and error responses.
findings.scenario: The allowlist contains only the case’s stable origin. A laboratory origin must be rejected consistently on the landing page, API and error responses.

findings.title: Retention period omits the calendar and starting event
findings.condition: The label thirty days does not say whether counting starts at creation, closure or publication, or whether it means calendar or working days. Two consumers produce different dates for the same case file.
findings.consequence: The ambiguity creates inconsistent retention decisions. The example establishes no legal periods and interprets no financial regulations.
findings.correction: Specify the starting event, time zone, calendar, duration and resulting date; version the rule and review exceptions with defined owners.
findings.scenario: The case file is created, closed and delivered on three different dates. The contract selects one as its starting point, and every consumer must obtain the same end date.

sections.body:
FICTIONAL CASE: the organization, people, assets, amounts and results are invented; no real systems were tested.

Grupo Atlas Servicios Financieros represents an invented banking group with personal and business channels, payments, documents, analytics and continuity. It does not correspond to an existing institution. The .example domains and documentation networks are not test targets. No real people, accounts, balances, cards or case files were queried.

The data exercises the composition of a long report: resource relationships, extensive tables, evidence images with different proportions, references, retests and publication decisions. Security observations belong to the scenario. Acceptance of the generator is recorded in a separate audit and is not presented as an outcome for the fictional bank.

An image called evidence is a synthetic representation. Commands are inert intent records, not executed instructions. Remediation states and approvals are also invented. This document certifies neither regulatory compliance, maturity nor universal absence of vulnerabilities.

version_history.author: Fictional Atlas team
version_history.notes: Extensive case, complete languages and fidelity criteria.

sections.distribution: Reusable example clearly identified as fictional. The Spanish, English and Portuguese variants include translated authored content; identifiers, domains, vectors and technical literals remain stable.

sections.summary:
Atlas represents an invented financial ecosystem comprising **28 assets, 60 findings, 7 analysis notebooks, 84 evidence images, 180 acceptance contracts and 10 root-cause groups**. Notebooks are not counted as vulnerabilities. The assessment describes conditions and decisions that can be traced from leadership to the responsible team. No banking operations were performed.

Scenario risk centers on three relationships: who may decide about a resource, which exact revision was authorized, and how business intent survives retries or recovery. Channel validation is insufficient to authorize every row in a batch. Approval of a request does not cover a recipient substituted later. A new message does not necessarily represent a new obligation either.

Identity mechanisms have different consumers. Session withdrawal must reach refresh credentials, delegations and temporary permissions; consent revocation must reach deferred jobs. These relationships need explicit contracts because local removal can coexist with old authorization in another queue, cache or backup.

Continuity is examined as recovery of content, state and restrictions. Restoring objects without their revisions, or reopening a queue without reconciling the ledger, can produce an available but inconsistent system. Acceptance therefore requires integrity checks, write authority and revocations made after the backup.

Analytical decisions need provenance and limitations. Missing values are not zero; a model label does not identify its parameters; a wall-clock timestamp does not establish causal order. The report retains those distinctions to avoid conclusions broader than the scenario evidence supports.

The governance proposal organizes actions by dependency. Authorization and business contracts are established first; producers and consumers then apply the same meaning; recovery, follow-up and publication are checked last. Plan durations are coordination assumptions, not commitments by a real company.

sections.posture:
Posture is described through verifiable invariants, without adding scores or turning them into a loss probability. CVSS bands reflect scenario assumptions, and informational observations are not vulnerabilities.

| Dimension | Trust boundary | Acceptance criterion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confidentiality | Subject, purpose and resource | Minimum access by revision and validity |
| Integrity | Obligation, currency and state | One intent produces a consistent result |
| Continuity | Backup, queue and authority | Reopening with reconciled content and policy |
| Traceability | Event, revision and evidence | An explainable decision without hidden inference |

An exception needs an owner, reason and expiry. Accepted status neither removes a finding nor demonstrates remediation; reported remediation does not replace a retest either. Blocking conditions and partial results remain visible in coverage.

sections.recommendations:
1. Resolve and authorize every resource within its organizational contract.
2. Bind approvals to immutable content and an independent identity.
3. Preserve obligation and revision across payments, retries and compensation.
4. Reconcile revocations and restrictions before recovering a service.
5. Version schemas, models and denominators used for analytical decisions.
6. Associate evidence and retests with specific closure criteria.
7. Separate private originals, the editable project and publishable derivatives.

Every recommendation needs a positive, a negative and a recovery check. Absence of visible errors alone does not demonstrate that every state or consumer shares the same policy.

sections.objectives:
Model interactions among channels, identity, payments, accounting, documents, third parties, analytics and continuity. The inventory contains twenty-eight assets with fictional owners and explicit relationships to findings and coverage.

The unit of analysis is a decision about a resource at a specific revision. Documentary scope does not amount to exploration of every endpoint or universal system coverage. The seven notebooks develop dependencies and review phases without claiming initial access or exploitation.
sections.assumptions: Only data created for this exercise is used. Network activity, credentials, personal information, transactions, social engineering, physical testing and availability testing of real services are excluded. Ports, responses and records are inert literals. References were not queried.

sections.approach: Each hypothesis documents a condition, consequence, correction, input scenario and three acceptance paths. Identifiers remain stable across languages, and narrative text is fully translated. Records distinguish description, fictional outcome and limitation.
sections.standards: CWE is used as an indicative classification and CVSS as a representation of assumptions. This document neither interprets nor establishes compliance with ISO, NIST, PCI DSS, banking legislation or any other standard.
sections.information_gathering: The inventory was created from scratch, without OSINT or external queries. CSV, Burp XML, Nuclei JSONL, Nmap XML and SARIF inputs are fabricated to exercise actual importers.
sections.enumeration: Assets, roles and model dependencies are described. A documentation address or invented port does not establish discovery of a service.
sections.exploitation: Intent records are inert text. There are no operational payloads, sessions, usable secrets or execution against the described destinations.
sections.post_exploitation: Impact chains are conceptual relationships between design decisions. No privilege escalation, persistence, extraction or lateral movement was performed.
sections.cleanup: The only changes are project files and outputs produced by report-gen. Generator checks remain separate from the scenario, and local servers must be closed when acceptance is complete.

sections.narrative:
### Chain A: resource, approval and obligation

[F01](#F01), [F02](#F02) and [F13](#F13) connect organizational isolation, approved content and idempotency. The scenario shows three separate barriers: selecting an authorized order, approving its revision and ensuring one business effect. This relationship does not demonstrate that all conditions are simultaneously reachable.

### Chain B: session, consent and document

[F07](#F07), [F19](#F19) and [F20](#F20) distinguish identity, purpose and object validity. Revoking one dimension does not ensure that its consumers have updated the others. Remediation requires shared semantics and checks on deferred paths.

### Chain C: delivery, privilege and recovery

[F25](#F25), [F31](#F31), [F37](#F37) and [F40](#F40) link approved content, administrative authority and reopening. Backup integrity does not ensure that permissions remain valid or that there is only one writer. Each boundary retains its own criterion.

### Chain D: data, decision and evidence

[F44](#F44), [F47](#F47), [F49](#F49) and [F51](#F51) distinguish model identity, completeness, correlation and evidence revision. Readable output may still be ambiguous if it loses one of those dimensions. No chain was executed against real infrastructure.

sections.overview:
The plan starts from ten root causes and avoids treating symptoms with isolated rules in every channel. Fictional teams coordinate contracts before changing consumers and preserve a rollback path compatible with current restrictions.

| Stage | Fictional owner | Dependency | Expected output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Architecture and identity | Stable object and subject | Explicit authorization contract |
| Transactions | Payments and accounting | Obligation and revision | Consistent states and idempotency |
| Consumption | Channels and third parties | Validity and purpose | The same policy at every consumer |
| Recovery | Continuity and platform | Manifest and revocations | Verifiable reopening |
| Follow-up | Independent review | Evidence and criterion | Dated result with limitations |
sections.short_term: Within seven fictional days, reduce unnecessary authority in the four critical hypotheses, establish revocation contracts and contain the highest-impact transitions. Agree who may accept an exception and what evidence they need.
sections.medium_term: Within thirty fictional days, align consumers of payments, consent, documents and sessions. Include negative and recovery cases in change reviews; check correlation and indicator denominators.
sections.long_term: Within ninety fictional days, rehearse integrated recovery and third-party contract termination in an authorized environment. Review dependencies, backups and derivatives with scoped evidence, avoiding confusion between task volume and effectiveness.

**Inputs:** a reproducible builder for YAML, synthetic PNG images and inert import files.

**Inspection:** validators and output review; external engines only inspect or render documents that have already been generated.
sections.glossary:
| Term | Use in the scenario |
| --- | --- |
| Obligation | Business intent independent of the transport message |
| Mandate | Permission with a subject, purpose, scope and validity period |
| Revision | Identity of the content or policy used for a decision |
| Derivative | Object produced from a source and subject to its lifecycle |
| Reopening | Decision to activate a service with reconciled restrictions |
| Retest | Fictional follow-up with a date, outcome and limitation |

sections.title: Decision governance and responsibilities
sections.body:
Scenario responsibility is distributed by decision, not merely by application. Channels present intent; identity establishes the subject and validity; payments transform an obligation; accounting retains its effect; continuity determines whether the assembly can reopen. Every handoff needs a contract and an owner who can explain its limits.

Conflicts between continuity and revocation are resolved before an incident. If an earlier backup retains withdrawn access, reopening cannot be based solely on availability. It must include reconciliation and an explicit exception when the procedure cannot be completed.

Risk acceptance belongs to a role distinct from technical verification. It can retain an open risk with a reason and expiry, but does not by itself turn a partial outcome into remediation. The record must distinguish these decisions when an executive summary is exported.

sections.title: Payment and multicurrency reconciliation contract
sections.body:
A payment intent contains an obligation, subject, beneficiary, currency, amount and revision. A message identifier tracks transport but does not necessarily identify a new intent. Queues and mobile applications may resend without creating another entitlement to payment.

The model separates authorization, reservation, execution, clearing and refund. Every transition supports retries with a stable response. If confirmation is lost, the consumer retrieves the durable result before deciding whether repetition is necessary. Compensation does not erase the history of the original decision: it adds a linked, explainable transition.

For cross-currency operations, the exchange rate is a versioned input. A new quote does not silently change an already accepted intent. Rounding retains precision, rule and adjustment, while reconciliation tables show differences with their origin rather than accumulating them under a generic category.

sections.title: Identity, delegation and revocation
sections.body:
A person’s or service’s identity is not the same as its session, browser or device. The scenario uses that distinction to prevent two sessions belonging to the same subject from simulating independence in an approval. Temporary roles also retain a grant with a purpose and expiry.

Revocation affects access families: short-lived sessions, refresh credentials, delegations, service credentials and deferred consumers. Every component must demonstrate what access withdrawal means and when it applies the decision. A successful central-catalog response does not prove that all consumers have converged.

Support must be able to help without gaining invisible authority. Delegated mandates identify who created them, which operations they allow and how they end. A change in account control requires reevaluation of those mandates, especially when recovery is initiated to remove suspicious access.

sections.title: Data purpose, retention and publication
sections.body:
The main document, its thumbnails, search excerpts and temporary exports belong to the same lifecycle even when stored in different systems. Policy must identify consumers and outcomes for each derivative. Deleting a catalog row does not demonstrate that all content has stopped being served.

An authorized purpose defines the minimum set of attributes. Schema evolution does not automatically grant permission for new columns. Publication compares allowed, required and prohibited fields and keeps exceptions visible when a consumer cannot yet apply the new rule.

The editable project may retain originals, private notes and control markers. Public delivery uses derivatives with explicit decisions. Structural PDF inspection is a partial aid and does not replace review of images, scanned content or semantic interpretations that require a person.

sections.title: Integrated recovery scenario
sections.body:
The conceptual exercise begins with backup C1, a later ledger and a queue containing messages that have already completed. After C1, a supplier is removed and a document classification changes. Those events require reconciliation of business state and access restrictions alike.

Recovery first checks manifest members, sizes and hashes. It then confirms dependencies and write authority. Only afterward does it reconcile obligations and revocations. If a required component is missing, output declares partial recovery and keeps reopening blocked for the affected flow.

Acceptance compares authorized and rejected cases. A current user must regain service; the retired supplier must remain without access; a completed obligation must not execute again. These conditions are recorded by revision so a later change can invalidate evidence without erasing its history.

sections.title: Data quality and decision explanations
sections.body:
Analytical data retains source, schema, units, times and completeness. A number without currency or scale can be syntactically valid and semantically wrong. Missing data must remain unknown when it reaches an executive indicator instead of turning into a reassuring zero.

Models and thresholds are identified by immutable versions. An alert explanation must refer to the parameters used for that decision, not current parameters under a reused label. Documentary reproduction preserves both revisions and their limitations.

Denominators are shown alongside indicators. Received, evaluated, rejected and pending records serve different purposes; combining them without explanation produces percentages that are difficult to compare. The scenario estimates neither accuracy, bias nor economic performance of a real model.

sections.title: Evidence and retest contract
sections.body:
Evidence provides information about a specific condition and revision. Its presence alone does not establish execution, completeness or remediation. This case uses synthetic images to exercise composition, captions, relationships and exports; each visibly declares that status.

Retests distinguish fixed, open, partial and unverified outcomes. Undated notes do not replace dated results, and a change communication does not automatically become verification. Records retain assessor, condition, outcome and limitation so a reader can determine what remained outside the scope.

Tables include allowed, rejected and recovery outcomes. A negative check must establish absence of an effect, not merely presence of an error message. Recovery must explain whether it retains one result and applies the restrictions in force when the service reopens.

sections.title: Annex C — Delivery, annexes and exclusions
sections.body:
Included annexes remain independent files within the delivery. No claim is made that the main PDF embeds their bytes. The editable project also retains private content, originals and synthetic publication controls.

{ANNEX_TABLE}

Annex review is recorded by hash and revision. Changing a file under the same name invalidates the earlier decision. PDF inspection is structural, bounded and does not include OCR; a partial result remains partial even when it finds no known marker.

Spanish, English and Portuguese versions retain identical IDs and relationships. Prose, evidence captions, synthetic images and annexes are fully localized. Technical tool names, paths, vectors and interoperability literals retain their original form.
